news.2026-10-22-arabie-saoudite-diplomat: Riyadh, Saudi Arabia
Riyadh
The US pulls non-essential diplomats out of Saudi Arabia as the Houthis keep striking
Washington is ordering non-emergency US government staff and their families to leave the kingdom. Attacks by the Houthis (rebels from Yemen) have hit airports and an oil field.
On 21 October the State Department ordered non-emergency US government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, in that country only [1][3].

According to Reuters, the order follows attacks: at least one dead and eight injured at the civilian airport in Dammam, and two dead in a drone attack on an oil field; earlier this month a strike on Riyadh's airport killed 12 and injured more than 300 [1][2].
Four US officials say missions in other Gulf countries will also ask families to leave [1]. US employees need special authorisation to use any airport in the country [3].
The first sentence to remember: when a country withdraws its diplomats, it is saying the security situation is worse than expected, even in a close ally that is a major oil producer [1][2].

The embassy had already been running with few staff for months, and the US military is quietly reducing its presence in the region, according to CBS [2][4]. For the economy, a riskier Gulf means pricier insurance and a jumpier oil market.
The Gulf supplies a large share of the world's oil. If travel, airports or oil fields there are under threat, petrol prices can rise even in France.

news.2026-10-22-liban-qatar-centrales-el: Beirut, Lebanon
Lebanon
Qatar offers Lebanon two power plants and twenty years of gas to end its blackouts
A draft plan seen by Reuters provides for two plants built within three years. Nothing is signed yet: both governments must approve it.
The draft, seen by Reuters, has Qatar building two gas-fired plants, at Deir Ammar (north) and Zahrani (south), of 825 megawatts each, within three years [1][2].
QatarEnergy would supply liquefied natural gas for 20 years, through a floating terminal and through the Arab Gas Pipeline that crosses Syria. The plan adds 800 MW of solar and 440 MW of wind [1][2].
Financing would come from private capital rather than Lebanese public money; payment terms are still to be negotiated. Prime Minister Nawaf Salam wants to bring the plan to the cabinet soon [1][3].
The first sentence to remember: Lebanon, broke and often in the dark, could see its electricity paid for by Qatar rather than by its own state [1][3].

This is a draft plan, not a contract: Beirut and Doha must both approve it, and Lebanese electricity plans have often stalled over tariffs and the management of the state utility [1]. The World Bank expects Lebanon's economy to shrink by 6.4% this year [4].
When a country has no reliable electricity, its businesses close and its people leave. Qatari gas flowing through Syria also shows how energy routes are being redrawn around the Strait of Hormuz.

news.2026-10-22-ghana-fin-exportation-mi: Accra, Ghana
Ghana
Ghana wants to stop exporting raw minerals by 2030: bauxite, manganese, iron and lithium
President Mahama announced it on Monday in Accra. Companies will have to process on site, but no law has been published yet.
On 19 October, at a mining summit in Accra, President John Dramani Mahama announced that Ghana will end exports of unprocessed minerals by 2030 [1][2].
It covers bauxite (the ore of aluminium), manganese, iron and lithium. Investors will have to fund processing on site, with these obligations written into their contracts [1][3].

No law, regulation or list of minerals has been published yet; Mahama promises legal measures and a transparent timetable [1][3]. The country already bans exports of scrap iron and non-ferrous metals [3].
The first sentence to remember: Africa's biggest gold producer wants to keep the added value at home instead of selling raw rock [1][4].

The idea is to get factories, jobs and more revenue, but it has a cost: processing needs electricity and investors ready to wait. For gold the direct effect would be limited, because large mines already melt their ore into bars (doré) before export [4].

Aluminium, manganese (steel) and lithium (batteries) end up in cars and smartphones. If several African countries copy Ghana, these materials may cost more to import raw, but would more often arrive already refined.

news.2026-10-22-burkina-faso-ghana-redui: Burkina Faso and Mali get only half their fuel: Ghana is keeping its own
Ghana's state distributor is cutting diesel and petrol sales to its landlocked Sahel neighbours. Burkina received only half of what it asked for.
Ghana's state distributor BOST has been cutting diesel and petrol exports to Burkina Faso and Mali since August, to protect Ghana's own supply [1][2].
For July and August, Burkina received only 40,000 tonnes of fuel out of the 80,000 it requested [3].
BOST's managing director sums it up: "Supply is available, but it's at a high cost" [2].
The first sentence to remember: two Sahel countries that call themselves sovereign depend on a coastal neighbour to keep their trucks and generators running [3].

Burkina Faso and Mali have no coastline: when a transit country keeps its fuel, prices rise and shortages follow. This tension comes in a world where oil is dearer because of the Hormuz crisis [1][3].
Missing fuel slows the gold mines and freight in the Sahel. That weighs on the gold and uranium leaving the region, and on migration when the local economy chokes.

news.2026-10-22-haiti-soldats-salvadorie: Haiti: four Salvadoran soldiers of the anti-gang force missing after an ambush
Their vehicle burned near Port-au-Prince. El Salvador is searching for its soldiers under gang fire.
Four Salvadoran soldiers of the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force fled their burning vehicle in Croix-des-Bouquets, north of Port-au-Prince, and are missing [1][2].
El Salvador's army says it has tried several times to reach them by land and air; its helicopters came under fire [1][2].

UN spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric condemned the attack and called for their release [1]. A wire story headlined on President Nayib Bukele reports that he is announcing a military operation to recover the soldiers [3].
The first sentence to remember: the international force meant to take Haiti back from the gangs is already losing men, and a Central American country finds itself on the front line [1][2].
The sources do not yet say whether the four are captive or hiding. The longer the attack lasts, the more the capital is cut off from the rest of the country, which blocks aid and goods [1][2].
Haiti is two hours by plane from Florida. When a state collapses, food runs short and departures by boat increase, which feeds the migration debates as far away as Europe.
news.2026-10-22-sri-lanka-chine-quitte-h: Sri Lanka: a Chinese state-owned firm drops its big logistics hub at the port of Colombo
The $392 million project goes on, but another investor has to be found.
China Merchants Port Holdings is pulling out of the logistics hub planned at the port of Colombo, Sri Lanka's port authority announced on 19 October, according to AFP [1][2].

The $392 million project, signed in 2023, gave 70% to China Merchants, 15% to the port authority and 15% to a Sri Lankan construction company [1][3]. The authority is looking for a new investor for the 150,000 m² site and will go through a public-private partnership [1][2].
The figures differ: a Sri Lankan outlet puts it at about $280 million [2]. China Merchants says ending the project is in the interest of the parties [1].
The first sentence to remember: a major Chinese group is giving up a project in Sri Lanka, a country China had helped and where it is very present [1][3].
It was the first big foreign investment announced after Sri Lanka's economy collapsed in 2022 [1][3]. China Merchants still operates a $500 million container terminal in Colombo [1].
Colombo is an important stop for cargo ships between Asia and Europe. When a port project stops, the rivalry between great powers over these routes becomes visible.

news.2026-10-22-inde-nouvelle-zelande-ac: India and New Zealand open their markets: wool and coal without tariffs
Their free-trade agreement was due to take effect on 20 October, after nine months of negotiations.
The agreement, signed in New Delhi on 27 April and ratified on 21 September, was due to apply from 20 October [1][2]. The sources consulted predate that date and do not yet confirm entry into force.
India gets tariff-free access for all its product lines; some Indian products used to pay up to 10% [1][3].
New Zealand says 57% of its exports to India, including wool and coal, will be tariff-free from day one, with a second round on 1 January 2027 [3][4].
The first sentence to remember: India is piling up trade deals just as American tariffs are changing the game [1][3].
The two countries want to roughly double their trade and have committed to review the deal one year after it takes effect [4].
When countries strike deals without going through the United States or Europe, trade routes diversify. In the long run, that can change where the wool, timber or medicines sold in France come from.

Belgium
Belgium: the prime minister says Brussels is dropping the use of frozen Russian assets for Ukraine
More than €190 billion of Russian money sits mostly in Belgium. Bart De Wever believes the European Commission will no longer propose using it.

Before the Belgian parliament, after the latest EU summit, Bart De Wever said he is confident the Commission will no longer propose funding Ukraine with Russian assets, according to the Russian agency TASS [1]. This is not an official Commission decision.
About €193 billion, at the end of September, is held mostly at Euroclear, a Belgian financial company [2].
In December 2025 the EU froze these assets indefinitely, and leaders chose to borrow €90 billion for Ukraine over two years [2][3].
The first sentence to remember: the idea of using frozen Russian money for Ukraine, which had divided Europe, seems to have been dropped in favour of borrowing [1][3].

Belgium feared Russian retaliation, since the money is held there. The information comes from a single dispatch from a Russian state agency: it needs confirmation from a Belgian or European source [1].
It is common European debt, so European public money, that funds aid to Ukraine, rather than frozen Russian money.

news.2026-10-22-arabie-saoudite-diplomat: Four years of truce, then the relapse

Since spring 2022, an informal truce had held between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, after years of war in Yemen and Houthi attacks on Saudi energy facilities [5]. On 13 July 2026, the Houthis fired missiles at Abha airport, in the south of the kingdom, accusing Riyadh of bombing an airport they control. It was the first claimed attack on the kingdom since the truce began [5].

Tensions had already risen in southern Yemen: in late 2025, a separatist movement backed by the United Arab Emirates took control of much of the south of the country [5]. In January 2026, the Emirates ended their counter-terrorism presence in Yemen after a Saudi strike hit vehicles belonging to their forces [10]. Yesterday's two allies are no longer playing the same game.

The escalation peaked on 10 October: the strike on Riyadh's King Khalid airport was the third that week on that airport. The 12 dead included four Saudis and people of seven other nationalities, among them one American [7]. The Riyadh-led coalition called it a war crime; the Houthis have not claimed this strike [6].
"Non-essential personnel": what the order really means

The State Department has two steps short of closing an embassy. The first, "authorized departure", is voluntary: staff and their families may leave at government expense, but those who wish can stay [8]. The second, chosen here, is "ordered departure": it is mandatory and is used to reduce the number of Americans on site [8]. Families then receive allowances to live elsewhere for the duration of the crisis [9]. The embassy itself stays open: only posts deemed indispensable (security, emergency consular services, leadership) remain filled. Moving from one step to the next is therefore a signal: Washington considers that the risk is no longer limited to a few incidents.
What could happen next
In the coming days
According to four US officials, other missions in the Gulf will also ask families to leave: the measure could spread beyond the kingdom [1].
The Saudi response
After the 10 October strike, the coalition promised to respond "firmly" [7]. A large-scale response could trigger new fire on Saudi cities.
Airports out of the conflict?
The Houthis say they are ready for reciprocal measures to keep airports, ports and humanitarian sites out of the fighting [7]. A limited deal of this kind would be a first step towards de-escalation.
Oil sites

The Houthis claim to have targeted two Saudi Aramco facilities, including the Khurais complex south-east of Riyadh; these claims have not been verified [11]. A confirmed attack on oil would be closely watched by markets.

The pipeline that was already supposed to fix everything

The idea of supplying Lebanon with gas via Syria is not new. The Arab Gas Pipeline, about 1,200 km long, was built in stages to export Egyptian gas to Jordan, Syria and Lebanon; gas reached Lebanon regularly from October 2009 [11].

The flow soon dried up: Egypt, consuming more and more, cut its exports, then attacks on the pipe during the war in Syria cut the route to Lebanon [13]. In 2021, ministers from four countries sought to revive the project to supply the Deir Ammar plant, with a capacity of 450 MW [12]. The World Bank was to finance the deal, but on condition that Lebanon raise its tariffs and create an electricity regulatory authority; with no regulator in place, it did not give the go-ahead [10].

In the meantime, EDL increased its output: at the end of February 2026, it supplied 7 to 9 hours of power per day on average. The regional oil shock brought it down again, to about two hours a day in some areas such as Tripoli [15]. According to L'Orient-Le Jour, the Syria-Lebanon section of the pipeline is still not in service and its repair is ongoing [14].
Who wants what
Doha

Qatar's prime minister, visiting Beirut on 16 October, announced a solar plant he described as "massive", developed by QatarEnergy with France's TotalEnergies as a first project [5]. The document seen by Reuters seeks to attract private capital [1].
Nawaf Salam's government
The prime minister says Qatar will finance, build and operate the project without the Lebanese Treasury advancing any money, and wants to put it to the Cabinet soon [5].
The World Bank and donors

For years they have tied their aid to reforms: raising tariffs that stayed low for decades and an independent regulatory authority in charge of setting prices and supervising contracts with the private sector [10]. In 2022, the average tariff collected was still under 1 cent per kWh, for a cost of about 30 cents [6].
news.2026-10-22-ghana-fin-exportation-mi: The Indonesian precedent: six years without raw nickel

The idea is not new. From 2014, Indonesia enforced a 2009 law banning exports of unprocessed ore, including nickel [5]. It reopened the door in 2017 to low-grade ore (under 1.7% nickel), then shut it completely on 1 January 2020 [6].

The result is striking. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, Indonesia's share of world nickel supply rose from 31.5% in 2020 to about 60% in 2024 [9]. Smelters multiplied, largely financed by foreign capital [8].

The verdict is still debated. President Joko Widodo claimed nickel-related exports had risen from 2.1 to 30 billion dollars; economists point out that these figures were never detailed and that a processed metal also includes the cost of energy and other inputs [8]. The European Union took the case to the WTO: the panel ruled in its favour on 30 November 2022, but Indonesia appealed on 8 December to an appellate body that no longer works, which blocks the case [7].
How it works: "processing locally"

An ore goes through several stages before becoming a metal. For aluminium: bauxite is mined, a refinery turns it into alumina (a white powder), then a smelter turns that into metal using a lot of electricity. Ghana has the start and the end of the chain, but not the middle: a bauxite mine at Awaso and the VALCO smelter in Tema, with no refinery. In 2022, all of Awaso's bauxite was therefore shipped abroad, while VALCO imported its alumina [11]. A ban on raw exports forces the missing link to be built at home. For manganese, the company running the Nsuta mine, a subsidiary of China's Tianyuan group, has presented a refinery project worth about 450 million dollars [13]. For gold, it is already done: since 1 September 2026, the doré gold of licensed traders must be refined in Ghana before export [16].

news.2026-10-22-belgique-avoirs-russes-g: How it works: frozen money that earns interest

Euroclear is a central securities depository: a kind of vault where central banks and investors around the world keep their bonds. When sanctions blocked the Central Bank of Russia in 2022, its securities stayed at Euroclear. When they mature, they do not pay Russia back: the money stays in Euroclear Bank's accounts, which will have to return it the day sanctions are lifted [6]. Euroclear reinvests this money, which earns it interest: 5 billion euros in revenue in 2025, down 26% as rates fell [5]. Since 2024, an EU rule requires these windfall profits to be paid into a fund for Ukraine: 6.6 billion euros paid by the end of March 2026, with the rest kept as a buffer against risks [4]. At the end of March 2026, out of Euroclear Bank's 237-billion-euro balance sheet, 200 billion were sanctioned Russian assets [4]. The "reparations loan", proposed by the Commission on 3 December 2025 for 165 billion euros [8], went further: the idea was to swap this money for EU-issued bonds and lend it to Ukraine, which would only have repaid it if Russia paid reparations [7].
Who says what
Belgium

Bart De Wever demanded that the 26 other countries guarantee the whole loan so that Belgium would not pay alone in case of a lawsuit [16]. In September 2026, his foreign minister Maxime Prévot still said that using these assets "through a process akin to confiscation" carried "significant risk" [10].
Supporters of using the assets

Poland, the Netherlands, Spain and Sweden wrote to the Commission in late August 2026 asking it to explore new ways of using these assets; EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the discussion would continue [10].
Ukraine
Volodymyr Zelensky wants all the assets to stay protected and usable, fearing they might one day be returned to Russia [11]. He has asked Europeans for about 78 billion dollars for next year [12].
Russia

Its central bank sued Euroclear in Moscow. On 15 May 2026, a Moscow court awarded it about 18.17 trillion roubles (200 billion euros); Euroclear does not recognise the court and has said it will appeal [13].
What could still move
Ukraine's 2027 budget
The 90-billion loan covers 2026 and 2027 [3]; Kyiv's new request raises the question of extra funding, and therefore of the Russian assets [12].
Next EU summits
According to De Wever, the Commission has committed not to reopen the file, but he does not rule out another country bringing it back to the table [14][15].
Euroclear's appeal
Euroclear is contesting the Moscow ruling and has said it will appeal; Russia's central bank itself considers the decision not final [13].
End of the war
European leaders decided the assets will stay immobilised until Russia ends the war and compensates Ukraine [9].
